extracted.intended_audience: recipients of federal education funds (K-12 and postsecondary institutions), Title IX coordinators, institutional legal counsel, OCR staff, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_short: Title IX grievance and pregnancy rules
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble discussion and final regulatory guidance for Title IX grievance procedures (appeals, informal resolution, Assistant Secretary review) and the definition/scope of 'pregnancy or related conditions,' including interaction with section 1688 (abortion neutrality) and Dobbs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required appeal bases (§106.46(i)(1)(i)-(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals may be offered on the bases specified in §106.46(i)(1)(i)-(iii) (as discussed: procedural irregularity affecting the outcome, new evidence that was not reasonably available at the time of determination, and decisionmaker bias or conflict of interest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department selected these three bases because each represents an error that, if left uncorrected, indicates the determination may be inaccurate. An appeal on bias can take into account whether a decision was against the weight of the evidence as part of a party's assertion of bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient discretion to offer appeals on additional bases
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may offer appeals on additional bases beyond the required bases (for example, an appeal of a remedy or sanction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a recipient decides to offer appeals on additional bases, both the complainant and respondent must have the opportunity to appeal on the same bases; offering appeals to one party but not the other (e.g., complainants but not respondents) would be inequitable and contrary to Title IX principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence and impartiality of appeal decisionmaker
rubrics_metrics.description: The decisionmaker for an appeal must not be the same person who investigated the allegations or dismissed the complaint and must be free from bias and conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final §106.45(d)(3)(iii) and §106.45(b)(2) (incorporated into §106.46(a)) require the appeal decisionmaker to review the underlying case independently, be free from bias/conflicts, and §106.8(d)(2)(iii) requires that the appeal decisionmaker be trained to serve impartially.

rubrics_metrics.name: No required appeal for simple/clear error or weight-of-evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declines to require appeals on the basis of simple error, clear error, or determinations being against the weight of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate case law indicates a lopsided or clearly erroneous outcome can support an inference of bias, but the regulations instead allow appeal on decisionmaker bias; bias-based appeals can consider whether a decision was against the weight of the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: New evidence standard for appeals (§106.46(i)(1)(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may appeal based on new evidence only if that evidence was not reasonably available at the time the determination or dismissal was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement guards against parties inappropriately withholding evidence during investigation to present it on appeal. The rule also recognizes many recipients may not use live hearings, so deeming all evidence not presented during investigation as forfeited could be inapplicable or overly restrictive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'determination' (not 'adjudication') to avoid implying live hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory language uses 'determination' rather than 'adjudication' in §106.46(i)(1)(i)-(ii) to avoid implying that a live hearing is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changing terminology to 'adjudication' could create inconsistency with §106.46(g) and unintentionally require live hearings; the Department declined to adopt that change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable treatment in appeal procedures (§106.45(b)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Regardless of how a recipient structures its appeal procedures, those procedures must treat complainants and respondents equitably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeal procedures must be consistent with §106.45(b)(1); the Department will provide technical assistance as appropriate to promote compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility for recipients in designing grievance procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients are granted flexibility and discretion to design and implement grievance procedures consistent with §§106.45 and, if applicable, §106.46.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients are often best positioned to know their communities' needs. The Department declined to provide more specific appeal procedure guidance at this time because procedures can depend on the basis for appeal and whether additional bases are allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal resolution optional (§106.46(j))
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may choose whether or not to offer informal resolution under §106.46(j).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department disagrees that §106.46(j) exceeds its authority and has not required that recipients offer informal resolution; related commenter concerns are addressed elsewhere (see §106.44(k) discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assistant Secretary (OCR) review scope (§106.47)
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.47 confirms that OCR (Assistant Secretary for Civil Rights) will not substitute its judgment for the recipient's decisionmaker regarding the weighing of relevant and not otherwise impermissible evidence in a particular case; §106.47 applies only to determinations whether sex-based harassment occurred under §106.45 and, if applicable, §106.46.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR will enforce the regulations consistent with its authority (20 U.S.C. 1682 and 34 CFR 100.7-11). OCR may hold recipients accountable for noncompliance with any Title IX provision (e.g., §106.31(a), (b)(4)). OCR will not require notice of private lawsuits nor routinely review private Title IX lawsuits; individuals may file complaints with OCR if they believe a recipient violated Title IX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'pregnancy or related conditions' (scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final definition includes 'pregnancy, childbirth, termination of pregnancy, and lactation, and all related medical conditions and recovery.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The definition is intentionally broad and inclusive, reflecting longstanding Title IX protection since 1975. The Department deleted the word 'their' in the recovery clause for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage not dependent on ADA disability status
rubrics_metrics.description: A pregnancy-related medical condition does not have to be a disability under the ADA to fall within the Title IX definition or to qualify for a reasonable modification under §106.40(b)(3)(ii).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections 106.10 and 106.40(b)(3)(ii) do not rely on the ADA; if pregnancy-related condition also meets ADA/Section 504 definitions, the individual has protections under those statutes as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection for perceived and potential pregnancy
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of 'pregnancy or related conditions' extends to discrimination based on perceived status and to 'potential' pregnancy (interpreted to cover expected, likely, or capacity to occur).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include discrimination against individuals seeking fertility care, planning to become pregnant, rumors about pregnancy, or assumptions that someone expected to become pregnant cannot participate in activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'or' for clarity ('pregnancy or related conditions')
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department changed the phrasing from 'pregnancy and related conditions' to 'pregnancy or related conditions' to match the defined term and be more accurate and inclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Or' covers being pregnant and also having a related condition, as well as someone only pregnant or only having a pregnancy-related medical condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid listing exhaustive medical conditions; provide examples
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declines to add a list of specific medical conditions to regulatory text to avoid implying that unlisted conditions are excluded; it acknowledges many conditions are related and provides examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include pregnancy-related fatigue, dehydration, nausea, increased body temperature, anemia, bladder dysfunction, gestational diabetes, preeclampsia, hyperemesis gravidarum, pregnancy-induced hypertension, infertility, recovery from childbirth/miscarriage/abortion, prenatal/postpartum depression, and lactation conditions such as swelling, leaking, or mastitis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'termination of pregnancy' (inclusive meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department interprets 'termination of pregnancy' to mean the end of pregnancy in any manner, including miscarriage, stillbirth, or abortion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Termination of pregnancy and medical conditions related to or recovery from termination are covered; Title IX prohibits discrimination against persons seeking, obtaining, or having experienced termination of pregnancy, subject to narrow limitations described (e.g., section 1688).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 1688 (Danforth Amendment) limits re: abortion benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1688 provides that nothing in Title IX 'shall be construed to require or prohibit any person, or public or private entity, to provide or pay for any benefit or service, including the use of facilities, related to an abortion,' and bars imposing penalties for seeking/receiving legal abortion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent with this limitation, Title IX does not require campus health centers to provide abortions or require student insurance to cover abortion even if other services are covered. However, the limitation is narrow and fact-specific; it does not authorize penalties that deprive unrelated rights or privileges because a person sought or had an abortion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on penalizing or retaliating for abortion when unrelated to providing abortion services
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1688 does not permit recipients to deprive someone of rights or privileges because they are considering, want to have, or have had a legal abortion, provided the right or privilege does not require the recipient to provide or pay for a benefit or service related to an abortion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a high school may not exclude a student from student council solely because she had an abortion; a college may not deny a professor a raise solely because she planned to have an abortion. Such adverse actions would constitute discrimination under section 1681 and section 1688 would not provide a defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiries about abortion circumstances can be discriminatory
rubrics_metrics.description: Inquiries into the circumstances of an abortion may be discriminatory if informed by sex stereotypes, handled differently than inquiries about other temporary medical conditions, or impermissibly deter someone from exercising Title IX rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients need not ask about specific circumstances and should avoid practices that create disparate treatment or chilling effects; handling must be consistent with protections for other temporary medical conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of section 1688 is fact-specific, not categorical
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether section 1688 limits Title IX beyond the described narrow ways depends on the particular facts and must be evaluated case-by-case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determinations about what section 1688 permits or limits require analysis of whether the issue involves a request for a recipient to pay for or provide a benefit/service related to abortion and whether denial would constitute a penalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dobbs does not alter Department's Title IX interpretation regarding termination of pregnancy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department states that Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization does not change its interpretation of 'pregnancy or related conditions' or 'termination of pregnancy,' nor its interpretation of Title IX's nondiscrimination mandate or section 1688.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department will offer technical assistance as appropriate to help recipients navigate interactions between Title IX obligations and State laws restricting abortion; the final regulations were not adopted in response to Dobbs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory authority for regulation (20 U.S.C. 1682; major questions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department asserts its authority under 20 U.S.C. 1682 and relevant precedent (e.g., Gebser) to promulgate regulations prohibiting sex discrimination under Title IX, including regulation of pregnancy or related conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department rejects arguments that regulating discrimination based on termination of pregnancy is beyond its authority or implicates the major questions doctrine; it considers the regulation within Congress' express delegation to the Department.
